content: In the 1970s and 1980s, the routine use of whole-cell pertussis (wP) vaccines was discontinued in certain countries due to concerns about adverse effects. Following this decision, there was a resurgence in cases of whooping cough. To address this issue, acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines were developed. These vaccines contain purified or recombinant antigens from Bordetella pertussis and were designed to be as effective as wP vaccines but with reduced reactogenicity. This review is an update of a Cochrane review first published in 1999 and last updated in 2012. No new studies were included in this update. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of acellular pertussis vaccines in children and to compare them with whole-cell pertussis vaccines. The search for relevant studies included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Biosis Previews, and CINAHL, covering publications up to January 2014. The review included double-blind, randomized trials that assessed the efficacy and safety of aP vaccines in children up to six years old. These trials required active follow-up of participants and laboratory confirmation of pertussis cases. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Due to differences in trial designs, a meta-analysis of efficacy data was not possible. However, safety data from individual trials were pooled using a random-effects meta-analysis model. The review incorporated six efficacy trials with a total of 46,283 participants and 52 safety trials involving 136,541 participants. Many of the safety trials did not adequately report methods for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, or blinding, making it challenging to assess the risk of bias. The efficacy of multi-component (three or more components) aP vaccines ranged from 84% to 85% in preventing typical whooping cough. Typical whooping cough was defined as 21 or more consecutive days of paroxysmal cough with laboratory confirmation of B. pertussis infection through culture, serology, or contact with a household member with culture-confirmed pertussis. For mild pertussis disease, characterized by seven or more consecutive days of cough with laboratory confirmation, the efficacy of multi-component aP vaccines ranged from 71% to 78%. In contrast, oneand two-component aP vaccines demonstrated lower efficacy, ranging from 59% to 78% for typical whooping cough and 41% to 58% for mild pertussis disease. Multi-component aP vaccines were found to be more effective than low-efficacy wP vaccines but may be less effective than the highest-efficacy wP vaccines. Regarding safety, systemic and local adverse events were significantly less common with aP vaccines compared to wP vaccines, both for the primary vaccination series and booster doses. In conclusion, multi-component (three or more components) acellular pertussis vaccines are effective in preventing whooping cough in children. They demonstrate higher efficacy than low-efficacy whole-cell vaccines but may not match the efficacy of the most effective whole-cell vaccines. Importantly, acellular vaccines are associated with fewer adverse effects compared to whole-cell vaccines, both during the primary vaccination series and with booster doses.
